extracted.intended_audience: Habitat for Humanity communicators, affiliate marketing/communications staff, and volunteers who produce external messaging (brochures, ads, press releases, social posts, ReStore materials)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for writing and designing external communications that convey Habitat for Humanity's unified brand story, tone, messaging, visuals and calls to action for U.S. audiences and local affiliates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Singular, unified brand story
rubrics_metrics.description: Create a singular, powerful Habitat story that engages hearts, minds and financial support; adopt a shared creative platform and unified messaging so Habitat is better known and understood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This guide exists to help create cohesive, consistent, clear and compelling messages and calls to action. Read the guide through for the big picture, then use it as a quick reference. Keep Habitat for Humanity as the primary, most-referenced brand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brand tone and personality
rubrics_metrics.description: Tone should be strong, determined and confident; not afraid to dig in, get dirty and lift others up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preferred tone descriptors: emotive, profound, urgent, inclusive, encouraging, solution-focused. Avoid: sad or sappy, preachy, overwhelming, 'us' vs. 'them', pushy, hopeless.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core narrative platform
rubrics_metrics.description: Build strength, stability and self-reliance through shelter — this is the central brand platform and story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the brand story statement: people partner with Habitat to build or improve a place they can call home; homeowners help build and pay an affordable mortgage; Habitat helps them achieve strength, stability and independence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core themes in messaging
rubrics_metrics.description: Emphasize the themes: strength, stability, self-reliance, shelter and a direct request for support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each word is intentional: 'building' reflects hands-on work; avoid softer words like 'dreams' or 'hope' as primary framing (though 'hope' or 'dignity' may be acceptable in moderation). Tie messages back to the core themes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Four key ingredients to any powerful brand story
rubrics_metrics.description: Include: (1) a critical need, (2) a definitive, specific role, (3) a lasting, meaningful outcome, and (4) a direct request for support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make stories specific to an individual or family, show solvable outcomes, and end with a clear, direct ask (donate, volunteer, speak up).

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience segmentation & targeting
rubrics_metrics.description: Know your audience: Successful Doers, Worldly Idealists, Social Influencers, Content Traditionalists, Showy Strivers — prioritize Successful Doers, Worldly Idealists and Social Influencers for growth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor messages to these segments when appropriate. Research-based profiles indicate what visuals and messages resonate; use that intelligence to select tone, facts and CTAs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know whether you're addressing EVERYBODY or SOMEBODY
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide if an audience is general (EVERYBODY) or specific (SOMEBODY) before crafting messaging.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If general (mainstream media, main website, mass social channels), keep to high-level messaging and language in this guide. If specific (niche blogs, grant proposals, targeted social posts), you may include more programmatic detail — but remain in concert with overall tone and keep Habitat as primary brand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make need specific, personal and solvable
rubrics_metrics.description: When describing need, avoid abstract or overwhelming global numbers; instead demonstrate tangible, personal need and show how an individual's support can help solve it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: large aggregate facts ('330 million households…') feel insurmountable. Better: localized or relatable figures (e.g., 'virtually nowhere in the U.S. can a full-time minimum-wage employee afford a one-bedroom apartment') and examples showing specific problems (mold causing asthma) that a small intervention can address.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid bleak, overly dramatic imagery/language
rubrics_metrics.description: Too bleak a tone or too stark images polarize audiences and reduce positive impressions of Habitat.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid 'sad puppy eyes' or imagery that feels like tragedy. Focus imagery and language on results and dignity rather than extreme need. Use examples and quotes that show impact rather than only suffering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasize homeowner partnership and agency
rubrics_metrics.description: Always position families as active participants: emphasize sweat equity, financial education and payment of an affordable mortgage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: People respond positively when they see homeowners 'helping themselves.' Explicitly state that homeowners help build and pay for their homes; this corrects misperceptions that Habitat simply 'gives houses away.' Use quotes and stories that demonstrate homeowner involvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize local and domestic work first
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever possible, emphasize local/domestic Habitat work to make impact relatable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Global scope gives credibility, but start with 'helping my neighbor first' for most general-audience communications. Local examples drive stronger engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious with framing like 'poverty housing' or 'break the cycle of poverty'
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid shorthand phrases about poverty that may not be the clearest or most universal ways to describe Habitat's impact for a general audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instead message: 'Habitat works to eliminate barriers to a better, healthier, more financially stable life' and describe outcomes (strength, stability, independence).

rubrics_metrics.name: Careful treatment of faith references
rubrics_metrics.description: Habitat is a Christian organization, but explicit faith references can be perceived as exclusionary to general audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use faith references carefully in general messaging. Direct homeowner/volunteer quotes that contain faith language are acceptable. Avoid prominent faith framing that could alienate potential supporters who are wary of religious ties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid surfacing advocacy/lobbying too early
rubrics_metrics.description: Discussing Habitat's advocacy or lobbying early or often in general-audience messaging can turn people off.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General audiences want emotional connection and tangible impact; complex policy discussions can be introduced later or to more targeted stakeholders who expect them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Facts about need: prefer relatable, lower-numbered or household-level facts
rubrics_metrics.description: High-performing facts make the issue personal and relatable; low-performing facts are large, aggregate global numbers that feel overwhelming.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use facts such as 'more than half of adults made tradeoffs to cover rent' or other stats that help an individual see themselves in the story. Avoid 'over 1.6 million families impacted' in isolation without personalizing context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Facts about impact: show homeowner-centered outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Use statistics that demonstrate how partnering with Habitat changes lives (e.g., kids' graduation rates, lower foreclosure rates) and frame homeowners as the actors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High-performing facts: 'Children of homeowners are 116 percent more likely to graduate from college' or foreclosure rates; avoid facts that present Habitat as sole actor or vague aggregate totals ('to date Habitat helped X people') without individual context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use first-person homeowner/volunteer quotes and gratitude
rubrics_metrics.description: Homeowner family gratitude and first-person impact stories are especially moving and persuasive for general audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer short, profound quotes showing appreciation and concrete outcomes. Let homeowners celebrate outcomes in their own words rather than over-describing emotional outcomes in organizational voice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct, specific calls to action
rubrics_metrics.description: Always incorporate a request for support — tell people Habitat needs money and make it easy for them to donate or get involved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit in CTAs, especially at moments of high motivation. Use actionable language and clear next steps (donate, volunteer, call, visit website).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use bite-sized currency framing for donation asks
rubrics_metrics.description: Present donation asks in small, specific amounts (e.g., $20/month) or tangible items (e.g., 'help with a roof') to make giving feel doable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: vague asks or very large totals. Concrete micro-level asks help people see their contribution as meaningful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep messaging at the appropriate level of detail
rubrics_metrics.description: For mass/general audiences, stay high-level; for niche/targeted audiences, provide more program detail — but always keep the overall tone consistent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of 'somebody' communications: targeted blogs, trade publications, grant proposals, or subject-matter expert tweets. Even when detailed, avoid letting program names or initiatives overshadow the parent brand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make Habitat the primary brand reference
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not let individual programs, events, or initiatives become the perceived brand; always describe them in relationship to the parent brand 'Habitat for Humanity.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If program names appear as often as or more than 'Habitat for Humanity', reset the copy. Use the parent brand name prominently and consistently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visual storytelling: show tangible results and dignity
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose images and video that show the positive outcomes of Habitat's work (strength, stability, families in their homes) rather than only extreme need.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid polarizing, tragic photos. Use photography and videography that demonstrate partnership, local impact, and solvable outcomes. When in doubt, prioritize photos that align with the tone: inclusive, encouraging, solution-focused.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be careful with numbers and timing in impact claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Large, headline-style numbers or long timeframes can feel like puffery or be hard to contextualize; use numbers to make the individual visible and believable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If using organizational totals, pair them with an individual story or local example; avoid presenting multi-million totals as the sole proof of impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language dos and don'ts
rubrics_metrics.description: Use plain, specific, human-centered language; avoid programmatic jargon, overly sentimental phrasing, or language that separates 'us' vs 'them'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do: emphasize 'we all' and shared humanity. Don't: use 'us' vs 'them' frames, preachy tones, or vague platitudes about 'giving hope' as the main outcome.
